questions.q: In Act I Scene i, the tribunes Flavius and Marullus scold the commoners because they
o: are celebrating Caesar's triumph over Pompey's sons
have refused to attend the Feast of Lupercal
questions.why: The tribunes remind the crowd that they once cheered Pompey, and accuse them of ingratitude.

questions.q: What warning does the Soothsayer give Caesar in Act I Scene ii?
o: 'Beware the man with the lean and hungry look.'
'Do not go to the Senate today.'
'Trust not the letters thrown at thy window.'
questions.why: The ides is the fifteenth of March; Caesar dismisses the Soothsayer as 'a dreamer'.

questions.q: Why does Caesar distrust Cassius?
o: Cassius once saved Caesar from drowning
Cassius refused to attend the races
Cassius has 'a lean and hungry look' and thinks too much
questions.why: Caesar judges that men who think too much and rarely smile 'are dangerous'.

questions.q: According to Casca, what happened when Antony offered Caesar a crown?
o: Caesar placed it on Brutus's head
The crowd took the crown away
Caesar refused it three times and then fell down in a fit
questions.why: Casca reports three refusals, each more reluctant, and Caesar collapsing with the 'falling sickness'.

questions.q: How does Cassius plan to win Brutus over at the end of Act I Scene ii?
o: By throwing letters, written in different hands, in at Brutus's window
By threatening to tell Caesar about Brutus
By offering Brutus a large sum of money
By asking Portia to persuade him
questions.why: The letters pretend that many Romans want Brutus to act against Caesar.

long.q: 'The fault, dear Brutus, is not in our stars, / But in ourselves, that we are underlings.' (a) Who speaks these lines, and when? (b) What does the speaker mean? (c) What is the speaker trying to persuade Brutus to do?
scheme: B1: (a) Cassius, to Brutus, in a public place during the Feast of Lupercal (Act I Scene ii), while Caesar is at the games
B1: (b) men are not ruled by fate; they can shape their own lives
B1: (b) so their being inferior to Caesar is their own fault, not destiny's
B1: (c) to join him in acting against Caesar before Caesar becomes king

long.q: Give the two incidents Cassius describes to Brutus to show that Caesar is physically weak.
scheme: B1: the swimming contest in the Tiber, when Caesar cried for help and Cassius saved him
B1: Caesar's fever in Spain, when he groaned and asked for drink 'as a sick girl'

long.q: Describe, in your own words, three of the strange sights reported in the storm of Act I Scene iii, and explain how Cassius interprets them.
scheme: B1: a slave's hand burned like many torches but was not scorched
B1: a lion near the Capitol glared at Casca and walked past without harming him
B1: men on fire were seen walking the streets, or an owl hooted at noon in the market-place
B1: Cassius says the heavens are warning of a monstrous state of affairs, that is, Caesar's growing power

long.q: 'Yond Cassius has a lean and hungry look; / He thinks too much: such men are dangerous.' What does this speech show about Caesar's judgement of people, and how is it ironic?
scheme: B1: Caesar is a shrewd judge of character; he correctly sees Cassius as discontented and dangerous
B1: yet he claims to fear nothing and does not act on his insight
B1: irony: Cassius is indeed planning his death, so the audience sees how close Caesar is to the truth

long.q: Explain the dramatic purpose of the opening scene (Act I Scene i).
scheme: B1: it shows the fickleness of the crowd, who once cheered Pompey and now cheer Caesar
B1: it reveals Caesar's great popularity with ordinary Romans
B1: it shows that some officials (the tribunes) already oppose Caesar, hinting at conflict
B1: it opens with humour (the cobbler's puns) and gives the background of Caesar's victory over Pompey's sons

questions.q: In his soliloquy in the orchard, Brutus compares Caesar to
o: a lion that has escaped its cage
a serpent's egg that should be killed in the shell
a star that has fallen from the sky
a tree that is already rotten
questions.why: Brutus admits Caesar has done no wrong yet, but fears what he may become, so he would kill him before he 'hatches'.

questions.q: Why does Brutus refuse Cassius's suggestion that Antony should be killed too?
o: He thinks Antony will join the conspiracy
He wants the conspirators to be 'sacrificers, but not butchers'
questions.why: Brutus thinks killing Antony would make the deed look bloody and calls Antony only 'a limb of Caesar'.

questions.q: How does Portia prove that she can be trusted with Brutus's secret?
o: She swears an oath on her father's name
She has given herself a voluntary wound in the thigh
questions.why: She says that bearing the wound patiently shows she can bear her husband's secrets too.

questions.q: What does Calphurnia dream?
o: Caesar's statue ran with blood like a fountain, and Romans bathed their hands in it
Caesar was crowned king at the Capitol
A lion attacked Caesar in the street
questions.why: Caesar reports the dream to Decius, who then gives it a flattering interpretation.

questions.q: How does Decius persuade Caesar to go to the Senate?
o: He threatens Caesar with a dagger
He calls the dream a good omen and hints that the Senate may mock Caesar if he stays at home
He tells Caesar that Calphurnia is lying
questions.why: He claims the blood means Rome will draw new life from Caesar and says a crown is to be offered that day.

long.q: 'Cowards die many times before their deaths; / The valiant never taste of death but once.' (a) Who says this, and to whom? (b) What has made the listener anxious? (c) What do these lines reveal about the speaker?
scheme: B1: (a) Caesar, to Calphurnia, on the morning of the ides of March (Act II Scene ii)
B1: (b) her terrifying dream and the strange sights reported in the night
B1: (c) Caesar's courage and refusal to show fear
B1: (c) but also his pride and arrogance, which lead him to ignore warnings

long.q: Why does Brutus refuse to let the conspirators swear an oath? Give his reasons.
scheme: B1: the wrongs of Rome should be motive enough to bind them
B1: the word of a Roman is enough; oaths are for cowards and deceitful men
B1: swearing would stain the virtue and nobility of their cause

long.q: Why does Brutus reject the idea of including Cicero in the conspiracy, and what does Cassius's reaction reveal?
scheme: B1: Brutus says Cicero will never follow anything that other men begin
B1: Cassius immediately gives way and drops the idea
B1: this shows Brutus taking over the leadership, and Cassius's need to keep Brutus at any price

long.q: How does Portia show that she is a worthy wife to Brutus in Act II Scene i?
scheme: B1: she has noticed his sleeplessness and changed behaviour and asks gently what is wrong
B1: she kneels and asks to share his secrets as his true wife, not a 'harlot'
B1: she reminds him she is Cato's daughter and Brutus's wife, stronger than other women
B1: she proves her constancy with the self-inflicted wound, and Brutus promises to tell her

long.q: In Act II Scene ii, Caesar invites the conspirators to 'taste some wine' with him before going to the Senate. Explain the dramatic irony of this moment.
scheme: B1: Caesar treats them as trusted friends
B1: the audience knows they intend to murder him within the hour
B1: Brutus's aside shows he is pained that their friendship is only an appearance, which deepens the tension

questions.q: A soliloquy is
o: a song sung by the chorus
a speech in which a character alone on stage speaks his or her thoughts aloud
a speech made to a crowd
questions.why: Brutus's 'It must be by his death' in the orchard is a soliloquy revealing his inner struggle.

questions.q: An aside is
o: a long speech by the hero
a stage direction for an exit
a brief remark heard by the audience but not by the other characters on stage
questions.why: Asides let the audience share a character's hidden thoughts during a conversation.

questions.q: Most of Julius Caesar is written in blank verse, which is
o: lines of varying length that rhyme alternately
questions.why: Blank verse has ten syllables a line in a da-DUM rhythm but no rhyme.

questions.q: Dramatic irony occurs when
o: the audience knows something that a character on stage does not
questions.why: Caesar greeting his murderers as friends is powerful because the audience knows their plan.

questions.q: The commoners in Act I Scene i speak mainly in prose. This suggests
o: that they are speaking to the gods
their low social status and everyday, informal speech
that the scene takes place at night
questions.why: Shakespeare often gives prose to common people and verse to nobles and serious moments.

long.q: Explain the part played by omens and the supernatural in Acts I and II of Julius Caesar. Refer to three examples.
scheme: B1: the Soothsayer's warning to beware the ides of March
B1: the terrible storm and strange sights reported by Casca
B1: Calphurnia's dream and the augurers finding no heart in the sacrificed beast
B1: effect: they create suspense and foreshadow Caesar's death, and show characters' attitudes (Caesar ignores them, Cassius uses them)

long.q: What is foreshadowing? Give two examples from Acts I and II of Julius Caesar.
scheme: B1: hints early in a play of events that will happen later
B1: example: Caesar's remark that Cassius is dangerous foreshadows the conspiracy
B1: example: Calphurnia's dream of Romans bathing their hands in Caesar's blood foreshadows the assassination

long.q: Distinguish between a soliloquy and an aside, and give an example of each from Julius Caesar.
scheme: B1: a soliloquy is a speech by a character alone on stage, revealing thoughts at length
B1: example: Brutus in his orchard deciding that Caesar must die (Act II Scene i)
B1: an aside is a short remark to the audience, unheard by others on stage
B1: example: Brutus's sad aside when Caesar calls the conspirators his friends (Act II Scene ii)

long.q: In Act I Scene i the cobbler calls himself 'a mender of bad soles'. Explain the pun and its effect.
scheme: B1: 'soles' (of shoes) sounds like 'souls', so he jokes that he mends bad souls
B1: the wordplay creates humour, shows the commoners' wit and irritates the tribunes

long.q: How does Shakespeare create tension in Act II Scene iv, where Portia waits with Lucius?
scheme: B1: Portia sends Lucius to the Senate but cannot tell him why, showing her confused anxiety
B1: she nearly gives away the secret, saying how hard it is for women to keep counsel
B1: the Soothsayer says he will wait to warn Caesar, reminding the audience that the murder is near

topics.name: Prose: plot, setting and narrative voice

questions.q: A story told by a character who refers to himself or herself as 'I' has
o: an omniscient narrator who is outside the story
questions.why: First-person narration gives one character's view, with only that character's knowledge.

questions.q: The setting of a story is
o: the time and place in which it happens
the last line of the story
questions.why: Setting includes the period, the place and often the social background.

questions.q: The exposition of a story
o: reveals the solution to the mystery
introduces the characters, setting and situation
is the moment of greatest tension
is the moral given at the end
questions.why: It comes first and prepares the ground for the conflict.

questions.q: Which is an example of internal conflict?
o: Two villages fighting over a well
A sailor caught in a cyclone
A boy torn between telling the truth and protecting his friend
A girl racing against a rival
questions.why: Internal conflict takes place inside a character's mind; the others are external.

questions.q: 'The bazaar was shutting down; shutters clattered, and the last rickshaw-puller dozed on his seat under a flickering bulb.' What mood does this setting create?
questions.why: Closing shutters, a dozing puller and a flickering bulb all suggest weariness and quiet.

long.q: Read this extract and answer the questions. 'I was twelve the summer my father's shop burned down. I did not cry then. I cried a year later, when I found his old account book in a trunk, his neat handwriting stopping halfway down a page.' (a) Who is the narrator, and how can you tell? (b) Why do you think the narrator cried a year later rather than at the time? (c) What does 'stopping halfway down a page' suggest? (d) Why is first-person narration effective here?
scheme: B1: (a) the shopkeeper's child, looking back as an adult; shown by 'I' and 'my father'
B1: (b) the shock was too great at first; the small, personal object brought the loss home
B1: (c) the father's work and life were cut short suddenly by the fire
B1: (d) it gives the reader direct access to the narrator's private grief

long.q: Explain the terms 'flashback' and 'climax', and say how each affects the reader.
scheme: B1: a flashback is a scene from an earlier time inserted into the story
B1: it gives background or explains a character's feelings
B1: the climax is the point of highest tension or the turning point
B1: it holds the reader's attention most strongly and decides the outcome

long.q: Distinguish between first-person and third-person narration, and give one advantage of each.
scheme: B1: first person: told by a character in the story using 'I'
B1: advantage: closeness to the narrator's thoughts and feelings
B1: third person: told from outside using 'he', 'she', 'they'
B1: advantage: can show several characters and events the main character does not see

long.q: Read: 'In the hills above Darjeeling, the mist came in every afternoon like a slow tide, swallowing first the tea bushes, then the factory chimney, then the road. By four o'clock Pema could not see the gate of her own school.' (a) Identify the simile and explain it. (b) How does the setting affect Pema? (c) What mood does the passage create?
scheme: B1: (a) 'like a slow tide': the mist rises steadily and covers everything as the sea covers a shore
B1: (b) she is cut off and cannot see her way home, which may make her anxious or isolated
B1: (c) a mysterious, closed-in or uneasy mood

long.q: Name, in order, the five stages of a typical plot and explain each briefly.
scheme: B1: exposition: characters, setting and situation introduced
B1: rising action: complications and conflict develop
B1: climax: the turning point of greatest tension
B1: falling action: the results of the climax unfold
B1: resolution: the conflict is settled and the story ends

questions.q: Direct characterisation is when
o: the writer states openly what a character is like
the reader must guess a character's name
a character speaks to the audience
questions.why: 'Mr Gupta was a mean man' is direct; showing him counting every paisa is indirect.

questions.q: Indirect characterisation reveals a character through
o: a list of adjectives at the start
speech, actions, thoughts and how others react to them
questions.why: Readers infer character from what people say and do.

questions.q: The theme of a story is
o: the order in which events happen
the place where it is set
a central idea it explores, such as courage, injustice or growing up
questions.why: Plot is what happens; theme is what the story is about at a deeper level.

questions.q: A round character is one who
o: is described as having a round face
is complex and may change during the story
questions.why: Round characters have several sides; flat ones have a single trait.

questions.q: 'Mrs Bose gave the beggar her lunch and then told her husband she had not been hungry.' This reveals that Mrs Bose is
o: generous and modest about her kindness
questions.why: She gives away her food and hides the sacrifice, showing quiet generosity.

long.q: Read: 'Leela found the purse outside the post office. Inside were two thousand rupees and a photograph of an old woman. She could have bought the cycle she had wanted for a year. Instead she walked to the police chowki, waited two hours on a bench, and refused the reward when the old woman's son arrived.' (a) What does this reveal about Leela's character? Give two qualities with evidence. (b) Why does the writer mention the cycle? (c) What theme does the passage suggest?
scheme: B1: (a) honest: she hands in the money instead of keeping it
B1: (a) unselfish or patient: she waits two hours and refuses the reward
B1: (b) to show that the temptation was real, which makes her honesty more admirable
B1: (c) honesty and integrity matter more than personal gain

long.q: What is meant by the theme of a story? How is it different from the plot? Give an example.
scheme: B1: theme is the central idea or message the story explores
B1: plot is the sequence of events; theme is what those events mean
B1: example: a story about a boy who saves a drowning rival (plot) explores forgiveness (theme)

long.q: Choose a character from a short story you have studied this year. Write a character sketch (about 200 words), referring closely to two incidents in the story. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: two or more clear character traits identified
B1: the first incident described accurately as evidence
B1: the second incident described accurately as evidence
B1: the character's speech or the reactions of others used as evidence
B1: change or development in the character discussed, where relevant
B1: organised paragraphs and accurate expression

long.q: Read: '"Leave it," said Arjun, as his little brother struggled with the knot. "I'll do it." He did not wait for an answer, and he did not see his brother's face fall.' What does this short exchange reveal about Arjun and his brother?
scheme: B1: Arjun is impatient or controlling (he takes over without waiting)
B1: he is not cruel but thoughtless; he does not notice his brother's feelings
B1: the brother wanted to manage on his own and is hurt or disappointed

long.q: Explain the difference between a static and a dynamic character, and suggest how a writer can show that a character has changed.
scheme: B1: a static character stays the same throughout the story
B1: a dynamic character changes in attitude or behaviour because of events
B1: change can be shown by contrasting the character's actions at the beginning and the end
B1: or through the character's thoughts, words, or others' reactions after a key event

topics.name: Poetry: imagery and figures of speech

questions.q: 'The moon is a silver coin dropped in a dark well.' The figure of speech is
questions.why: The moon is said to be a coin, without 'like' or 'as'.

questions.q: 'The wind howled like a hungry wolf.' The figure of speech is
questions.why: The comparison uses 'like'.

questions.q: 'The sunflowers turned their faces to follow the sun.' This is an example of
questions.why: Flowers are given human faces and a human action.

questions.q: 'I have told you a million times to close the gate!' This is
questions.why: It is a deliberate exaggeration for emphasis.

questions.q: Imagery in a poem is
o: the number of lines in each stanza
language that appeals to the senses to create pictures in the reader's mind
the pattern of rhyme at line ends
questions.why: Images can appeal to sight, sound, smell, taste or touch.

long.q: Read these lines (written for this question) and answer: 'The sky lets down its long grey hair, / the gulmohar shakes off its red, / and every tin roof in the lane / drums out a song above my head.' (a) Identify and explain the figure of speech in line 1. (b) What does line 2 describe? (c) Which sense do lines 3–4 appeal to, and how? (d) What mood do the lines create?
scheme: B1: (a) personification or metaphor: the falling rain is pictured as a woman's long grey hair
B1: (b) the red flowers of the gulmohar tree being shaken down by the rain
B1: (c) hearing: rain drumming on the tin roofs like music
B1: (d) a lively, joyful or refreshing mood of the monsoon

long.q: Explain the difference between a simile and a metaphor, and give an original example of each.
scheme: B1: a simile compares two things using 'like' or 'as'
B1: a suitable original simile
B1: a metaphor says one thing is another, without 'like' or 'as'
B1: a suitable original metaphor

long.q: Read (lines written for this question): 'Grandfather's hands are maps / of rivers he has crossed, / of fields that he has ploughed and sown, / of harvests won and lost.' (a) Explain the metaphor in line 1. (b) What kind of life do the lines suggest? (c) What is the effect of repeating 'of'?
scheme: B1: (a) the lines and veins of his hands record his life as a map records places
B1: (b) a long, hard-working farming life with successes and failures
B1: (c) it builds a list that stresses how many experiences his hands carry

long.q: Identify the figure of speech in each: (a) 'The stars danced on the lake.' (b) 'Life is a long road.' (c) 'Silent and still, the snow settled on the sleeping town.' (d) 'O river, why do you hurry so?'
scheme: B1: (a) personification
B1: (b) metaphor
B1: (c) alliteration (repeated 's' sounds)
B1: (d) apostrophe (addressing something that cannot answer)

long.q: What is a symbol in poetry? Explain how a lamp might be used as a symbol in a poem about hope.
scheme: B1: a symbol is an object that stands for an idea beyond itself
B1: a lamp gives light in darkness
B1: so it can stand for hope that lasts through hard times, e.g. a lamp kept burning for someone's return

questions.q: What is the rhyme scheme of these lines (written for this question)? 'The road was long and grey, / the night came on too soon, / we walked the hours away / beneath a paper moon.'
questions.why: Grey and away rhyme (A); soon and moon rhyme (B), alternating.

questions.q: A couplet is
o: two consecutive lines of poetry, usually rhyming
questions.why: Couplets often round off a poem or a stanza.

questions.q: Which line contains alliteration?
questions.why: The repeated 's' sound at the start of several words is alliteration.

questions.q: Enjambment is
o: a pause in the middle of a line
the running on of a sentence from one line to the next without a pause
the repetition of a line at the end of each stanza
a rhyme within a single line
questions.why: It creates flow or suspense by carrying the meaning over the line break.

questions.q: The tone of a poem is
o: the number of syllables in each line
the poet's attitude to the subject, such as mocking, mournful or joyful
questions.why: Tone is shown through word choice, imagery and rhythm.

long.q: Read the stanza (written for this question): 'At dawn he pushes from the muddy shore, / the river grey as an unwritten slate; / his oar dips, rises, dips once more, / and the far bank waits, as it always waits.' (a) Give the rhyme scheme. (b) What does the rhythm of line 3 imitate? (c) What is the effect of repeating 'waits' in the last line?
scheme: B1: (a) ABAB (shore/more; slate/waits as a near rhyme)
B1: (b) the regular, repeated movement of the oar in the water
B1: (c) it suggests patience and the endless sameness of the ferryman's routine

long.q: What is a refrain? Explain two effects it can have in a poem.
scheme: B1: a line or phrase repeated at intervals, often at the end of each stanza
B1: it emphasises the central idea or feeling
B1: it gives the poem a song-like rhythm and makes it memorable

long.q: Read (written for this question): 'Clang goes the gate, and crunch go the feet / of children who hurry and scurry and meet / at the corner where Ramu sells ices and sweets.' (a) Identify two examples of onomatopoeia. (b) Find an internal rhyme. (c) What atmosphere do the sounds create? (d) How does the rhythm suit the subject?
scheme: B1: (a) 'clang' and 'crunch'
B1: (b) 'hurry' and 'scurry'
B1: (c) a noisy, cheerful, busy atmosphere of children leaving school
B1: (d) the quick, bouncing rhythm matches the children's hurrying movement

long.q: What is a sonnet? Name its two main types and describe how each is structured.
scheme: B1: a poem of fourteen lines, usually in iambic pentameter
B1: the Petrarchan (Italian) sonnet has an octave of eight lines and a sestet of six
B1: the Shakespearean (English) sonnet has three quatrains and a final couplet
B1: usual rhyme schemes: ABBAABBA + CDECDE (or similar) and ABAB CDCD EFEF GG

long.q: Read the stanza (written for this question) and comment on its tone, giving evidence: 'I folded my childhood into a tin trunk, / the cricket bat, the letters, the torn kite; / my mother packed the pickles, and then sank / onto the step, and did not say goodnight.'
scheme: B1: the tone is sad, tender or quietly sorrowful
B1: 'folded my childhood' suggests leaving a whole stage of life behind
B1: the mother 'sank' onto the step, showing grief she cannot speak
B1: the plain ending 'did not say goodnight' is understated, which makes the emotion stronger

questions.q: Just before the assassination, Metellus Cimber kneels to Caesar to
o: ask for a post in the army
plead for his banished brother to be recalled
questions.why: Caesar refuses, and the conspirators use the petition as a pretext to crowd round him.

questions.q: In refusing the petition, Caesar compares himself to
o: the northern star, which never moves
questions.why: 'I am constant as the northern star' shows his pride just before he is struck down.

questions.q: Why does Cassius object to Antony speaking at Caesar's funeral?
o: He thinks Antony is a poor speaker
He fears the people may be moved by what Antony says
questions.why: Cassius rightly judges that Antony could turn the crowd against them.

questions.q: In his funeral speech, Brutus says he killed Caesar
o: not because he loved Caesar less, but because he loved Rome more
questions.why: Brutus, speaking in prose, appeals to the crowd's reason and patriotism.

questions.q: According to the will that Antony reads, each Roman citizen is to receive
questions.why: Caesar also leaves his private gardens and orchards on the near side of the Tiber to the public.

long.q: 'Et tu, Brute? Then fall, Caesar!' (a) At what moment are these words spoken? (b) Why does Caesar single out Brutus? (c) What do the words reveal about Caesar's feelings?
scheme: B1: (a) as the conspirators stab Caesar in the Capitol, when Brutus strikes
B1: (b) Brutus was his close and trusted friend, so his betrayal hurts most
B1: (c) Caesar gives up the struggle once he sees Brutus among his killers, showing his love for and trust in him

long.q: State the conditions on which Brutus allows Antony to speak at Caesar's funeral.
scheme: B1: Antony must speak from the same pulpit, after Brutus has finished
B1: he must not blame the conspirators
B1: he may speak all the good he can of Caesar
B1: he must say that he speaks by the conspirators' permission

long.q: How does Antony turn the crowd against the conspirators in his funeral speech? Refer to the techniques he uses.
scheme: B1: he pretends to have come only to bury Caesar, claiming he is 'no orator, as Brutus is'
B1: he repeats 'Brutus is an honourable man' until the phrase becomes ironic
B1: he disproves the charge of ambition (the refused crown, ransoms filling the treasury, weeping for the poor)
B1: he holds back the will to stir curiosity, then reveals Caesar's generosity
B1: he shows the torn mantle and the body, naming the 'most unkindest cut' of Brutus
B1: he appeals to emotion, pausing in tears ('My heart is in the coffin there with Caesar')

long.q: 'O, pardon me, thou bleeding piece of earth, / That I am meek and gentle with these butchers!' (a) When does Antony speak these lines? (b) Why does he ask pardon? (c) What does he prophesy in the rest of the speech?
scheme: B1: (a) alone with Caesar's body, after the conspirators leave (Act III Scene i)
B1: (b) for pretending friendship with the murderers
B1: (c) civil war and bloodshed across Italy
B1: (c) Caesar's spirit, with Ate, will 'Cry Havoc!' and let slip the dogs of war

long.q: What is the dramatic significance of the killing of Cinna the poet in Act III Scene iii?
scheme: B1: he is killed only because he shares a name with a conspirator ('Tear him for his bad verses')
B1: it shows the blind fury of the mob that Antony has stirred up
B1: it marks Rome's slide into lawlessness and the fickleness of the crowd

questions.q: At the start of Act IV, the three men who now rule Rome are
questions.why: They form the triumvirate and draw up a list of enemies to be put to death.

questions.q: What does Antony think of Lepidus?
o: He is the wisest of the three
He is a slight, unmeritable man, fit only to be sent on errands
He is the true heir of Caesar
He is a brave soldier who should lead them
questions.why: Antony plans to use Lepidus and then discard him, like an ass that carries gold.

questions.q: When Brutus says Cassius has 'an itching palm', he means that Cassius
o: is greedy for money and sells offices for bribes
wants to shake hands and make peace
questions.why: Brutus is angry that Cassius has defended an officer condemned for taking bribes.

questions.q: How did Portia die?
questions.why: Brutus tells Cassius she grew desperate at his absence and the enemy's growing strength.

questions.q: When Caesar's ghost appears to Brutus at Sardis, it says that
o: Brutus will see it at Philippi
questions.why: The ghost calls itself Brutus's 'evil spirit' and foreshadows his defeat.

long.q: 'There is a tide in the affairs of men, / Which, taken at the flood, leads on to fortune.' (a) Who says this, to whom, and in what situation? (b) What does the speaker mean? (c) What does Cassius want to do instead, and why does he give way?
scheme: B1: (a) Brutus to Cassius, in Brutus's tent at Sardis, while deciding whether to march to Philippi
B1: (b) opportunities must be seized at the right moment or they are lost
B1: (c) Cassius wants to wait and let the enemy tire themselves out marching to them
B1: (c) Brutus argues that their own forces are at their peak while the enemy grows; Cassius yields to keep the peace

long.q: What are the causes of the quarrel between Brutus and Cassius in Act IV Scene iii?
scheme: B1: Brutus condemned Lucius Pella for taking bribes, ignoring Cassius's letters pleading for him
B1: Brutus accuses Cassius of having an itching palm and selling offices
B1: Cassius refused Brutus gold to pay his legions
B1: Cassius feels Brutus no longer loves him and treats him as a lesser man

long.q: How is the quarrel resolved, and what does it reveal about each man?
scheme: B1: Cassius offers Brutus his dagger and bares his breast; both admit fault and shake hands
B1: Brutus reveals that Portia is dead, which explains his temper
B1: Brutus is principled but self-righteous
B1: Cassius is emotional and dependent on Brutus's love and respect

long.q: What does Act IV Scene i reveal about Antony?
scheme: B1: he is ruthless: he agrees to his own nephew's death in the list of the condemned
B1: he plans to cut down the legacies in Caesar's will, though he used the will to win the people
B1: he is scornful and manipulative towards Lepidus, using him as a tool

long.q: What is the dramatic purpose of the appearance of Caesar's ghost in Act IV?
scheme: B1: it shows that Caesar's spirit remains powerful after his death
B1: it foreshadows Brutus's defeat and death at Philippi
B1: it reflects Brutus's troubled conscience and adds to the tragic atmosphere

questions.q: Cassius takes his own life because he believes that
o: Titinius has been captured by the enemy
questions.why: Pindarus wrongly reports that Titinius has been surrounded and taken.

questions.q: The sword with which Pindarus kills Cassius
o: is the same sword that Cassius used to stab Caesar
questions.why: Cassius dies saying that Caesar is revenged 'even with the sword that killed thee'.

questions.q: How does Brutus die?
o: He is killed by Antony in single combat
He runs on his own sword, which Strato holds for him
questions.why: His friends refuse to help him, but Strato agrees after asking for Brutus's hand.

questions.q: Antony calls Brutus
questions.why: Antony recognises that only Brutus acted for the common good, not from envy.

questions.q: On the day of the battle at Philippi, Cassius reminds Messala that it is
questions.why: He dies on the day he was born, which adds to the sense of fate completing a circle.

long.q: 'This was the noblest Roman of them all.' (a) Who speaks these words, and over whom? (b) Why, according to the speaker, did the other conspirators act? (c) Why was this man different? (d) What does the speaker mean when he says 'the elements' were so mixed in him?
scheme: B1: (a) Antony, over the body of Brutus at Philippi
B1: (b) the others acted out of envy of great Caesar
B1: (c) he alone acted honestly, for the common good of Rome
B1: (d) his qualities were perfectly balanced, so Nature could say 'This was a man!'

long.q: Describe the mistake that leads to Cassius's death.
scheme: B1: Cassius sends Titinius to find out whether some troops are friends or enemies
B1: Pindarus, watching from the hill, reports that Titinius has been surrounded and taken
B1: believing this, Cassius orders Pindarus to kill him
B1: in fact the horsemen were friends; Titinius returns with a wreath of victory and kills himself beside Cassius

long.q: 'O Julius Caesar, thou art mighty yet! / Thy spirit walks abroad.' Explain the context and significance of these lines.
scheme: B1: Brutus speaks on finding the bodies of Cassius and Titinius
B1: they have died by their own swords, as if Caesar's spirit is taking revenge
B1: the lines express a key idea: Caesar dominates the second half of the play though he dies in Act III

long.q: How does Brutus meet his death, and what do his last words show?
scheme: B1: he asks Clitus, Dardanius and Volumnius to help him die, and they refuse
B1: Strato holds the sword and Brutus runs upon it
B1: his last words tell Caesar to be still, since he kills himself more willingly than he killed Caesar
B1: they show remorse or a sense that justice is done, and his choice of death over capture shows Roman dignity

long.q: What happens at the parley before the battle in Act V Scene i, and how does it show Octavius's growing authority?
scheme: B1: the generals exchange insults; Antony says the conspirators flattered Caesar like fawning hounds while planning his murder
B1: Cassius reminds Brutus that Antony would not be insulting them if Cassius had been allowed to have him killed
B1: Octavius vows to fight until Caesar's wounds are avenged
B1: Octavius insists on leading the right wing against Antony's wish, showing he will not take orders

topics.name: Drama: Julius Caesar, themes and characters

questions.q: Brutus's tragic flaw is often said to be
o: his idealism, which makes him misjudge other people's motives
questions.why: He assumes others share his noble aims, so he spares Antony and trusts the crowd.

questions.q: Most critics regard the tragic hero of the play as
questions.why: Brutus is a noble man brought down by a flaw, and his inner conflict runs through the play.

questions.q: The fickleness of the crowd is shown most clearly when the plebeians
o: cheer Brutus and then, minutes later, riot against the conspirators
questions.why: Within one scene they want to crown Brutus and then hunt him down.

questions.q: Which pair of scenes most clearly contrasts Portia and Calphurnia as wives?
o: Act I Scene i and Act V Scene v
Act II Scenes i and ii
Act III Scenes ii and iii
Act IV Scenes i and ii
questions.why: Both wives plead with their husbands, back to back, on the night before the ides.

questions.q: Brutus's funeral speech is in prose while Antony's is in verse. The main effect is that
o: Brutus seems more emotional than Antony
Antony's speech is shorter and plainer
Brutus appeals to reason, while Antony appeals to emotion
questions.why: Brutus's balanced prose argues; Antony's verse moves the crowd to tears and fury.

long.q: Write a character sketch of Cassius, referring closely to the play. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a shrewd judge of men who sees through others (e.g. reads Caesar and Brutus well)
B1: envious and resentful of Caesar's rise (the Tiber and Spain stories)
B1: a skilful manipulator (the forged letters thrown in at Brutus's window)
B1: practical and politically wiser than Brutus (wants Antony killed, opposes the funeral speech) but yields to him
B1: capable of deep affection and emotion (the quarrel and reconciliation)
B1: rash in the end, killing himself on a mistaken report, on his birthday

long.q: 'Julius Caesar is a play about the conflict between public duty and private feeling.' Discuss with reference to Brutus. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: Brutus loves Caesar personally ('I love him well')
B1: his soliloquy in Act II shows him choosing what he thinks Rome needs over friendship
B1: he justifies the murder publicly: he loved Rome more than Caesar
B1: private cost: his sleepless anguish and the strain on Portia
B1: his grief over Portia's death, hidden while he plans the war, shows duty overriding feeling
B1: a balanced conclusion: the conflict makes him a tragic figure

long.q: Brutus makes three crucial errors of judgement. Identify them and explain the consequences of each.
scheme: B1: sparing Antony's life against Cassius's advice
B1: consequence: Antony survives to lead the revenge
B1: allowing Antony to speak at the funeral, and to speak last
B1: consequence: Antony turns the mob against the conspirators, who must flee Rome
B1: insisting on marching to Philippi instead of waiting
B1: consequence: they meet the enemy on poor terms and are defeated

long.q: Who is the real hero of the play, Caesar or Brutus? Give reasons for your view.
scheme: B1: a clear stand
B1: a reason supported by the play (e.g. Brutus has the inner conflict and noble flaw of a tragic hero)
B1: a second supported reason (e.g. Caesar dies in Act III, yet his spirit drives the action to the end)
B1: the other view acknowledged and answered

long.q: Explain the role of the supernatural in Julius Caesar as a whole.
scheme: B1: warnings before the murder: the Soothsayer, the storm and portents, Calphurnia's dream
B1: the ghost at Sardis promises a meeting at Philippi
B1: these build suspense and an atmosphere of doom
B1: they raise the question of fate against free will, which Cassius and Brutus argue about

questions.q: In an extract-based question, 'Give the context' means you should
o: give the author's date of birth
say where in the story the extract comes and what has just happened
questions.why: Context places the extract: who is involved, at what point, and why the moment matters.

questions.q: '"What a lovely day for a picnic," said Father, as the rain hammered on the car roof.' This is an example of
questions.why: Father says the opposite of what the situation is, which is verbal irony.

questions.q: Why might a writer end a story without resolving its conflict?
o: Because the writer ran out of space
To leave readers thinking about the issue for themselves
Because every story must end that way
To make the plot easier to follow
questions.why: An open ending invites the reader to judge or imagine what happens next.

questions.q: 'Every evening she lit the lamp in the window, though her son had been gone for ten years.' The lamp most likely symbolises
o: her hope that her son will return
questions.why: Keeping a light burning for someone suggests stubborn hope and love.

questions.q: When a question says 'with close reference to the text', you should
o: give a summary of a different story
support each point with brief details or quotations from the story
questions.why: Examiners reward points backed by precise evidence.

long.q: Read this extract (written for this question): 'The headmaster held up the broken window pane. "Who did this?" Nobody moved. Then Sameer, who had been nowhere near the playground, stood up. Behind him, Rohit stared at his shoes.' (a) What has probably happened? (b) Why might Sameer have stood up? (c) What does 'stared at his shoes' suggest about Rohit? (d) What dilemma will Sameer and Rohit now face?
scheme: B1: (a) someone has broken a school window and nobody will own up
B1: (b) to protect the real culprit, perhaps his friend Rohit, or to end the tension
B1: (c) Rohit is guilty and ashamed
B1: (d) Rohit must decide whether to confess; Sameer whether to take the punishment for his friend

long.q: Read (written for this question): 'For thirty years, Miss D'Souza had taught the same poem to Class Six. This year she closed the book halfway through, looked out of the window at the rain, and said, "Let us write our own."' (a) What does the first sentence suggest about Miss D'Souza's teaching? (b) Why is the rain mentioned? (c) What change does the last sentence show, and why is it significant?
scheme: B1: (a) it had become routine and unchanging
B1: (b) it may inspire her or suggest a fresh, cleansing change of mood
B1: (c) she breaks her habit and invites the children to be creative
B1: (c) it suggests a moment of renewal, both for her and her class

long.q: Read (written for this question): 'The landlord's car stopped at the edge of the field. He did not get out. He rolled the window down two inches, enough to speak, not enough to let in the dust.' What does this reveal about the landlord and his attitude to the farmers? Refer to two details.
scheme: B1: he does not get out of the car, which shows he keeps himself apart from the farmers
B1: he opens the window only 'two inches', which suggests coldness or contempt
B1: 'not enough to let in the dust' shows he sees the farmers' world as dirty and beneath him
B1: overall: he is proud, distant and indifferent to those who work his land

long.q: Explain the difference between situational irony and dramatic irony in a short story, and give an example of each.
scheme: B1: situational irony: the outcome is the opposite of what is expected
B1: example: a fire station burns down
B1: dramatic irony: the reader knows something a character does not
B1: example: the reader knows the gift has already been sold, while the character still plans for it

long.q: Read (written for this question): 'When the dam was built, the village went under the water. Now, in the dry months, when the lake shrinks, the top of the temple appears, and old Kamala walks out across the cracked mud to light a lamp on it.' (a) What happened to the village? (b) Why does the temple reappear only in the dry months? (c) Why does Kamala light a lamp there? (d) What theme does the passage suggest?
scheme: B1: (a) it was flooded when the dam was built
B1: (b) the water level falls in the dry months, uncovering the temple's top
B1: (c) out of faith and memory of her lost home
B1: (d) the human cost of development, or loss and memory

topics.name: Prose: theme, message and extended responses

questions.q: Which of these is a theme rather than a plot event?
questions.why: A theme is an idea; the other options are things that happen.

questions.q: A writer's message is
o: the name of the main character
the view or lesson about life that the story leaves with the reader
a letter that appears in the plot
the title printed on the cover
questions.why: Messages are often implied through what happens to characters.

questions.q: In a long answer on a story's theme, a strong paragraph should
o: retell the whole plot in order
make a point, support it with evidence from the story and explain the evidence
questions.why: Point, evidence and explanation shows understanding, not just memory.

questions.q: A story set in a village during a drought explores the effect of poverty on a family. The setting mainly helps to
o: show that the writer likes villages
create the pressures that drive the characters' choices
questions.why: Setting often sets up the conflict that reveals theme.

questions.q: A story ends with a once-proud man apologising to the servant he mistreated. The ending most likely suggests
o: that pride can be overcome by humility and recognition of others' worth
that servants should never be trusted
that the man is planning revenge
questions.why: A change in the character at the end often carries the story's message.

long.q: Choose a short story you have studied in which a character faces injustice. Explain how the writer presents the injustice and what message the story conveys (about 250 words). (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: the story and character identified, with the injustice described accurately
B1: how the writer presents it: one technique with evidence (e.g. contrast, irony, viewpoint)
B1: a second technique or incident with evidence
B1: the character's response analysed
B1: the story's message stated clearly
B1: organised answer in accurate, formal English

long.q: Read (written for this question): 'Ajay's father had driven an auto-rickshaw for twenty years so that Ajay could study. On the day Ajay received his engineering degree, his father waited outside the hall, in his khaki uniform, because he thought he would not be allowed in.' (a) What sacrifice has the father made? (b) Why does he wait outside? (c) What theme does the passage raise? (d) How does the detail of the 'khaki uniform' strengthen it?
scheme: B1: (a) twenty years of hard work driving an auto-rickshaw to pay for his son's education
B1: (b) he feels his work and class make him unwelcome in such a place
B1: (c) parental sacrifice, or class barriers and dignity of labour
B1: (d) it marks him as a working man and shows the social gap between him and the graduates

long.q: Explain how a writer can use the title of a short story to point to its theme. Give an example of a title you might choose for a story about a lonely old man and a stray dog, and explain your choice.
scheme: B1: the title can name a key symbol, object or idea that carries the theme
B1: it can prepare the reader or create irony when read again after the ending
B1: a suitable title (e.g. 'Company')
B1: explanation linking the title to the theme of loneliness and friendship

long.q: 'The best stories make us see ordinary people differently.' With reference to one story you have studied, explain whether you agree. (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: a clear stand
B1: the story and the ordinary character identified
B1: how the writer makes the reader look again at that character, with evidence
B1: a second piece of evidence
B1: a reasoned conclusion

long.q: What is the difference between a story's subject and its theme? Illustrate with a story about a girl who wins a cycle race against boys.
scheme: B1: the subject is what the story is about on the surface (a cycle race)
B1: the theme is the deeper idea it explores
B1: e.g. challenging gender stereotypes, or determination overcoming prejudice

questions.q: Read (written for this question): 'The clock above the blackboard does not care. / It ticks for those who know and those who guess.' The clock is
o: personified as indifferent to the students
questions.why: 'Does not care' gives the clock a human attitude, showing that time moves on regardless.

questions.q: In the same lines, the contrast between 'those who know and those who guess' suggests
o: only clever students can hear the clock
the clock is guessing the time
time passes the same for prepared and unprepared students alike
questions.why: The clock treats everyone equally, which raises the tension of an exam.

questions.q: Read (written for this question): 'the forty pens that scratch, and pause, and press.' The commas mainly
o: show that the poet has made a mistake
slow the line down to imitate the stop-start rhythm of writing
questions.why: Each pause matches a moment of thinking between bursts of writing.

questions.q: Read (written for this question): 'Below the flyover, the city hums / a lullaby of horns and engines low.' Calling traffic noise 'a lullaby' is
o: an unexpected image that makes the noise sound soothing
a direct description of a mother's song
questions.why: The metaphor turns harsh sounds into something familiar and calming at night.

questions.q: When asked how a poet creates a mood, the best answer
o: only says the poem is good
names a technique, quotes it briefly and explains its effect
questions.why: Technique, evidence and effect together earn full marks.

long.q: Read the stanza (written for this question): 'Forty years of strangers in his boat, / their bundles, quarrels, prayers and songs; / he hears them all, and keeps afloat, / and carries none of it for long.' (a) Who is 'he'? (b) What does the list in line 2 suggest? (c) Explain the double meaning of 'carries' in the last line. (d) What attitude to life does the ferryman have?
scheme: B1: (a) an old ferryman who has rowed passengers for forty years
B1: (b) the great variety of people and human experiences he has seen
B1: (c) he carries passengers across the river but does not carry their troubles in his mind
B1: (d) calm acceptance or detachment; he listens but lets things go

long.q: Read (written for this question): 'They cut the neem tree on a Tuesday; / by Wednesday the birds had gone; / by Thursday no one could remember / where the shade had fallen on the lawn.' (a) What is the effect of naming the days? (b) What does the last line suggest about people? (c) What is the poet's tone?
scheme: B1: (a) it shows how quickly the loss happens and is forgotten, day by day
B1: (b) people forget what they have lost very fast, even something that gave them comfort
B1: (c) quietly sad or regretful, with a note of criticism

long.q: Read (written for this question): 'Below the flyover, the city hums / a lullaby of horns and engines low; / a chaiwala counts out his coins and drums / his fingers on the kettle's dying glow.' (a) What time of day is described? How do you know? (b) Find an example of alliteration. (c) What impression of the chaiwala is given? (d) What is the effect of 'dying glow'?
scheme: B1: (a) late night: the 'lullaby' and the kettle's fading heat at the end of the day
B1: (b) e.g. 'counts out his coins' (hard 'c' sound)
B1: (c) a tired, patient worker finishing a long day, perhaps a little restless or bored
B1: (d) the fire is going out, suggesting the end of the day and of his energy

long.q: Read (written for this question): 'I folded my childhood into a tin trunk, / the cricket bat, the letters, the torn kite.' (a) Explain the metaphor in line 1. (b) Why are these particular objects chosen? (c) What is the significance of the kite being 'torn'?
scheme: B1: (a) leaving childhood behind is pictured as packing it away in a trunk
B1: (b) they are everyday, personal objects that stand for games, friendships and memories
B1: (c) it suggests that childhood joys are already damaged or ending, or that they are precious despite being imperfect

long.q: Read (written for this question) and answer: 'The clock above the blackboard does not care. / It ticks for those who know and those who guess; / it ticks across the hush, the held-in air, / the forty pens that scratch, and pause, and press.' (a) Where is the poem set? (b) Explain 'the held-in air'. (c) Identify the rhyme scheme. (d) How does the poet create tension?
scheme: B1: (a) in an examination hall
B1: (b) the students are so tense that they seem to be holding their breath
B1: (c) ABAB
B1: (d) the indifferent ticking clock, the silence and the stop-start writing build pressure

questions.q: The central idea of a poem about an old banyan tree outliving everyone who planted it is most likely
o: the endurance of nature beyond human lives
the history of a city council
questions.why: The tree's long life set against human lifetimes points to permanence and change.

questions.q: A poem that describes war using cheerful, marching rhythms and then ends with a list of the dead is probably
o: ironic, using the contrast to criticise war
questions.why: A mismatch between rhythm and subject often signals irony.

questions.q: The 'speaker' of a poem is
o: the voice that speaks in the poem, which may not be the poet
the person who reads it aloud in class
questions.why: Poets often write in the voice of a character, a child or even an object.

questions.q: A shift in tone in the last stanza of a poem often signals
o: a change in the speaker's feelings or a new understanding
the start of a new poem
that the poem has no theme
questions.why: Look for words like 'but' or 'now' that mark the turn.

questions.q: When writing an appreciation of a poem, you should comment on
o: theme, tone, imagery, sound and form, and how they work together
questions.why: A full appreciation links the poem's methods to its meaning.

long.q: Write an appreciation (about 200 words) of these lines written for this question: 'At dawn he pushes from the muddy shore, / the river grey as an unwritten slate; / his oar dips, rises, dips once more, / and the far bank waits, as it always waits.' (Mark yourself with this scheme.)
scheme: B1: the subject and theme identified (routine, patience, the passing of time)
B1: the simile 'grey as an unwritten slate' analysed (each day blank, full of possibility or sameness)
B1: the rhythm of line 3 linked to the rowing
B1: the repetition of 'waits' and its effect discussed
B1: the tone described with evidence (calm, reflective)
B1: a personal response supported by the text

long.q: Compare the tone of these two sets of lines written for this question: A: 'The sky lets down its long grey hair, / the gulmohar shakes off its red.' B: 'They cut the neem tree on a Tuesday; / by Wednesday the birds had gone.'
scheme: B1: A is joyful or celebratory
B1: evidence from A, e.g. the playful personification of the sky and tree
B1: B is sad, flat or regretful
B1: evidence from B, e.g. the plain listing of days, which makes the loss seem matter-of-fact

long.q: Explain how the form of a poem (stanza length, rhyme, line length) can support its meaning. Give one example.
scheme: B1: regular stanzas and rhyme can suggest order, routine or calm
B1: broken lines or irregular rhyme can suggest disorder or strong emotion
B1: a suitable example linking form to meaning (e.g. short lines for sudden shock)

long.q: 'A poem about a small, everyday thing can carry a large idea.' Explain this statement with reference to the lines 'I folded my childhood into a tin trunk, / the cricket bat, the letters, the torn kite' (written for this question).
scheme: B1: the everyday subject: packing a trunk before leaving home
B1: the large idea: growing up and leaving childhood behind
B1: the ordinary objects act as symbols of memories
B1: so a small scene carries a universal feeling that readers recognise

long.q: What is meant by the 'speaker' and the 'tone' of a poem? Explain why it is important not to confuse the speaker with the poet.
scheme: B1: the speaker is the voice or persona that speaks in the poem
B1: the tone is the attitude of that voice to the subject
B1: poets often adopt a voice unlike their own, so treating every 'I' as the poet can lead to a wrong reading
